segments.speaker: A
segments.text: I'm Marcus, and this is Iris. A camera-trap team is choosing a board. Vendor A quotes eight TOPS at eight-bit integer. Vendor B quotes fifteen TOPS at four-bit. Vendor C quotes latency on a proprietary model, Vendor D cites a benchmark score from two generations ago, and Vendor E gives only peak throughput at maximum batch. Which board wins?

visual.title: Which claim survives normalization?
visual.alt: Five spec cards quote 8 TOPS INT8, 15 TOPS INT4, a proprietary latency, a two-generation-old MLPerf score and a peak at maximum batch. All five must be normalized onto the same task, model, state and boundary before the camera-trap gates decide.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: None of them can win yet, and that's the first lesson of this chapter. Each card names a different measurement — different precision paths, different models, different rules, different machine states. A rate in TOPS and a latency on an unknown model aren't two answers to one question. They're answers to five different questions.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: The fix is the chapter's core move: turn a claim into a test. Fix the task and dataset — what counts as correct. Fix the model and metrics — what counts as better. Fix the harness that executes and records, the machine specification, and the run rules a reproduction must match. Only then does the output become a number you can argue with.

visual.title: A claim becomes a test
visual.alt: A claim enters six fixed components — task and data, model and metrics, harness, machine specification, run rules and report — and exits as a number that can be argued with a measurement.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Run rules are where honest benchmarks spend their effort. Warm-up policy, clock and power state, cache state, repetition count, and which initialization work is timed. A cold cache and a warm cache are different machines.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Before any of that, the chapter opens with the scale of the gap. An H100 delivers nine hundred and eighty-nine teraflops of dense sixteen-bit arithmetic at peak. ResNet-50 training at about five thousand images per second per accelerator — the rate a sixty-four-accelerator system logged in MLPerf Training — sustains about a hundred and twenty-three.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: That's a model FLOPs utilization of about twelve percent. The peak is a ceiling under favorable state. MFU reports what the run actually achieved — and the gap between them is where memory-bound layers, the input pipeline, and launch overhead live.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Prediction and measurement complement each other here. The roofline puts ResNet-50's ceiling near forty thousand images per second against the ridge. The benchmark reports five thousand. The floor tells you where to look; the measurement tells you what the machine did.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: The same dilution shows up inside a single request. Take a pipeline with eight milliseconds of preprocessing and ten of inference. Make inference five times faster and the total goes from eighteen to ten — a one-point-eight-times gain, not five. Even infinitely fast inference leaves the eight milliseconds it never touched.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: That's why component speedups need end-to-end verification. The chapter's edge board is the same story: an attached accelerator runs the model seven and a half times faster than the host CPU, but the user sees about three times, because preprocessing never leaves the host.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: For serving, the mean hides the operative failure. If one percent of requests take ten times longer, that's ten thousand slow requests per million — timeouts and churn measured at the ninety-ninth percentile, invisible at the mean. Report the percentiles, and for generative work report time to first token and time per token separately.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Cold start is another number users actually feel. A seven-billion-parameter model in sixteen-bit is about fourteen gigabytes. A PCIe-4 transfer at twenty-five gigabytes per second takes about five hundred and sixty milliseconds before the runtime does any work — that's the floor that makes model caching a design requirement.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Energy follows one identity — power times time — and every ambiguity lives in which power and which window you integrate. Google's median assistant prompt drew zero point one watt-hours at the accelerators and zero point two four counting everything the service needs. Same prompt, same machines. Only the meter boundary moved.

visual.title: One prompt, two measurements
visual.alt: The same prompt costs 0.10 Wh measured at the accelerators and 0.24 Wh measured across the whole service: 58 percent active accelerators, 25 percent host CPUs and DRAM, 17 percent idle reserve and overhead.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Two point four times from the boundary alone — fifty-eight percent accelerators, twenty-five percent host CPUs and DRAM, seventeen percent idle reserve. And precision is an energy lever, not just a size one: decomposing MobileNetV2, the float32 weight read and the compute cost comparable joules; eight-bit takes the total from forty-four hundred microjoules to about seven hundred.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Battery life follows the duty cycle. Keyword spotting runs one inference per one-second window — about eight milliseconds of work per thousand, under a one-percent duty cycle. At that duty, standby power sets the drain. The efficiency that matters is the one that's off.

visual.title: 8.3 ms of work per 1,000 ms
visual.alt: Inside each one-second audio window the DS-CNN inference runs for 8.3 milliseconds — a 0.8 percent duty cycle. At that duty the standby floor, not the 3.3 millijoule inference, sets the battery drain.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Average power is duty times active plus one minus duty times standby. The crossover where active energy starts to matter sits well above the operating duty for always-listening workloads.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Then comes the statistics. A compressed model scores ninety-four percent where the baseline scores ninety-five on the same thousand images — fifty errors versus sixty. Under an independent-samples model the difference is within noise. So is the regression real?

eq.title: Standard error of an accuracy difference

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: The marginals can't answer it. The paired comparison can: count where the two models disagree. Images they both get right or both get wrong carry no information — McNemar's test asks whether the disagreements are lopsided enough to be real, and at most twenty-six disagreements still flag this gap.

visual.title: Same scores, different disagreements
visual.alt: Both illustrative runs have 50 baseline errors and 60 compressed-model errors on 1,000 images. Count which model alone was right. With the chapter’s uncorrected McNemar statistic, 10 against 0 gives 10.0, above the 3.84 cutoff. With 30 against 20 it gives 2.0, below the cutoff.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: And one more way a number stops meaning what it claimed: Goodhart's law. A team raised beam search from one to ten, gained half a BLEU point, and turned fifty milliseconds into two hundred — the metric improved and the product broke. Benchmarks are targets.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: So back to the five vendor cards. What do we actually do with them?

visual.title: Which claim survives normalization?
visual.alt: Five spec cards quote 8 TOPS INT8, 15 TOPS INT4, a proprietary latency, a two-generation-old MLPerf score and a peak at maximum batch. All five must be normalized onto the same task, model, state and boundary before the camera-trap gates decide.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Use them for a shortlist, then run one test. Fix the trap's own frames, the deployed model artifact, a sustained thermal state at the deployment duty cycle, and a full-stack meter boundary. Measure the ninety-ninth-percentile frame time, energy per frame, and recall on the species the study cares about. The card that survives normalization is the answer — and it might not be the fifteen-TOPS one.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: A benchmark is evidence under conditions, never proof. The only question that survives contact with production is whether those conditions matched.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: And this chapter is where the whole optimization part of the book cashes out — data selection, compression, acceleration all ended on a favorable local number. Benchmarking is the discipline that checks whether the numbers survive.
